name: POEditor
tagline: Manage translation keys, contributors, suggestions, and standard file exports

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 1,000 strings; unlimited projects; up to 5 contributors; rate-limited API

tiers.name: Plus
tiers.limits: 10,000 strings; unlimited projects and contributors; workflows

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: 30,000 strings; unlimited projects and contributors; broader automation/integrations

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: 100,000 strings; unlimited projects and contributors; SSO
tiers.notes: $234/mo equivalent when billed every 6 months; custom higher limits available.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 1,000 strings total across all projects, unlimited projects, and up to 5 contributors
pricing.hiddenCosts: The string count is the sum of source terms and translations across every hosted project; upgrading mid-cycle charges the prorated difference.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For POEditor, manage translation keys, contributors, suggestions, and standard file exports. The hard boundary is hosted collaboration, integrations, translation memory, and simple workflow, plus translation memory, collaboration, and deployment integrations.
coreLoopDIY: Manage translation keys, contributors, and suggestions, preserve context, import and export standard files, and publish approved strings.
requirements: optional DeepL or OpenAI API key
whatYouLose: hosted collaboration, integrations, translation memory, and simple workflow
moatNotes: translation memory, collaboration, and deployment integrations
ongoingBurden: file formats, placeholders, plural rules, screenshots, context, permissions, review, glossary, machine translation, sync, and backups
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for POEditor because localization teams pay because language context, review discipline, translators, and release integrations are the hard parts. The recurring cost buys file formats, placeholders, plural rules, screenshots, context, permissions, review, glossary, machine translation, sync, and backups, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Tolgee
priorArt.desc: Active open-source localization platform with translation memory and in-context tooling.

alternatives.name: Tolgee
alternatives.desc: Keys, contributors, comments, review and normal localization formats, plus in-context editing POEditor never had.

facts.install: Hosted Tolgee Cloud signup or the official Docker Compose deployment with PostgreSQL
facts.engines: Tolgee's contextual AI translator and machine-translation layer can connect to Google Cloud Translation, Amazon Translate, DeepL, Microsoft Azure Translator, Baidu, and configured LLM/MT providers.
facts.dataFormat: Self-hosted projects, keys, translations, users, and translation memory live in PostgreSQL, while screenshots and uploaded files live under the persistent data directory; cloud accounts store the same classes of data on Tolgee infrastructure.
facts.gapVsPaid: Tolgee is more capable but also more complex, and POEditor remains easier for a non-technical contributor to join, translate, export, and leave without operating infrastructure.
facts.setupBlocker: None for cloud signup; self-hosting needs Docker, an external PostgreSQL database, persistent file storage, mail/domain/TLS, backups, and provider keys for third-party translation engines.

alternatives.name: Weblate
alternatives.desc: Contributor translation, suggestions, checks, review and broad file-format support tied neatly to version control.

facts.install: Hosted Weblate signup or the official Docker Compose deployment
facts.engines: Machine translation can connect to OpenAI/Azure OpenAI, DeepL, Google Cloud, Amazon Translate, Microsoft Translator, LibreTranslate, Baidu, Yandex, and other documented services.
facts.dataFormat: Translations, users, review state, memory, glossaries, and settings live in PostgreSQL; cloned source repositories and uploaded files live in persistent server volumes, with Valkey/Redis used for queues and caches.
facts.gapVsPaid: Weblate's repository-first model and administration are heavier than POEditor's simple hosted contributor workflow and can be disproportionate for a small catalog.
facts.setupBlocker: Cloud hosting is free only for qualifying libre projects; the general free route requires Docker, PostgreSQL, Valkey/Redis, domain/TLS, mail, repository credentials, backups, and upgrades.

alternatives.name: Accent
alternatives.desc: A smaller collaborative string editor with history and exports; enough product, considerably less platform.

facts.install: Run the published Docker image with an external PostgreSQL database and production environment variables
facts.dataFormat: Projects, languages, strings, translations, comments, history, and users live in PostgreSQL; application configuration and secrets live on the server.
facts.gapVsPaid: Accent lacks POEditor's polished hosted onboarding, broad import/export coverage, translation-memory and suggestion depth, contributor management, and low-maintenance operation.
facts.setupBlocker: The first obstacle is a production Elixir web deployment with Docker, external PostgreSQL, SECRET_KEY_BASE and authentication configuration, TLS, mail, backups, and upgrades; the old standalone Accent CLI is archived.

alternatives.name: Ever Traduora
alternatives.desc: A clean team translation catalog with suggestions, search, imports, exports and an API.

facts.install: Official Docker Compose deployment; Kubernetes and source-build paths are also documented
facts.dataFormat: Projects, terms, translations, teams, suggestions, and API credentials live in the configured PostgreSQL/MySQL database, with configuration and logs on the server.
facts.gapVsPaid: Ever Traduora requires self-hosting and has a smaller file-format, integration, translation-memory, and contributor-management surface than POEditor.
facts.setupBlocker: A non-expert has to configure Docker, the database, environment secrets and the initial administrator, then add HTTPS, mail, backups, and upgrades.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Start plan and a small-team string-management system DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for POEditor in an empty repository.
Use Next.js 15, TypeScript, PostgreSQL, Drizzle ORM, and one optional machine-translation API; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: manage translation keys, contributors, and suggestions, preserve context, import and export standard files, and publish approved strings.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Implement projects, locales, keys, namespaces, descriptions, screenshots, translations, and review status.
Import and export JSON, YAML, PO, and XLIFF while preserving placeholders and plural forms.
Add glossary checks, missing-string filters, translation memory, comments, and reviewer assignment.
Use machine translation only on selected strings and show provider, cost, and source text before approval.
Provide token-authenticated pull and push endpoints for CI with an immutable change log.
Add backups, locale deletion safeguards, and a pseudo-localization preview.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a translator labor marketplace.
Deliberately leave out a global website translation proxy.
Deliberately leave out enterprise integrations, legal translation assurance, and round-the-clock support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
